title: The long view
intro: Start far back. A year is easier to judge once you can see the ten around it.
questions: Ten years ago, what did you think your life would look like by now?
The gap between that picture and today shows what changed: you, or the plan.
Which decision from the last ten years shaped your life the most?
Big turns are easier to see from a distance.
What did you want badly five years ago that no longer matters to you?
Wanting changes. That is a reason to look twice at what you want today.
What have you kept doing for years, even when nobody asked you to?
What you keep returning to is usually what you value.
Which friendship or relationship has lasted the longest, and why has it?
It tells you what you need from people.
What is the hardest thing you have come through, and what did it leave you with?
You are more durable than one bad month suggests.
When in your life did you feel most like yourself?
This is your reference point for a life that fits.
What did you believe about work or money ten years ago that you have since dropped?
Old rules often keep running long after you stop believing them.
Which place you have lived or worked suited you best?
Surroundings matter more than most of us admit.
What skill have you built slowly that you now take for granted?
Slow progress is invisible until you look back.
Whose advice turned out to be right?
It shows whose voice is worth listening for.
What risk are you glad you took?
Keep it as evidence for the next one.
What risk are you glad you did not take?
Caution deserves credit too.
What have you been saying "one day" about for more than five years?
A "one day" either needs a date or needs letting go.
If you met yourself from ten years ago, what would surprise them most about you now?
A quick way to see how far you have come.

title: The last twelve months
intro: Now the year itself. Go month by month in your head, or open your calendar and your photos to jog your memory.
questions: If this year were a chapter in a book, what would its title be?
Naming the year makes you decide what it was about.
Which three moments from this year would you keep?
What you would keep shows what to make more of.
What did you finish this year?
Finished things are forgotten faster than unfinished ones.
What did you start and quietly drop?
No blame. Dropped things show where the plan or the timing was wrong.
Where did most of your time actually go?
Time is the most honest record of your priorities.
Where did most of your money go, beyond the bills?
The same question, in a different ledger.
What gave you energy this year?
This is what to protect next year.
What drained you this year?
Do less of it, or change how you do it.
Who did you see more of this year, and who did you see less of?
People drift in and out without anyone deciding.
What was the best decision you made this year?
Look at how you made it, so you can do it again.
What would you do differently if you had the year again?
Regret is useful once, as an instruction.
What did you learn about yourself that you did not know in January?
A year that taught you nothing has not been looked at closely enough.
What were you worried about a year ago that turned out fine?
It is a check on how well your worries predict anything.
What did you say yes to that you should have turned down?
This shows where your limits are soft.
What are you proud of that nobody else noticed?
Private wins count.

title: Where you are today
intro: The past is done. These questions are about this week and what is missing from it.
questions: How would you describe your life right now to a close friend, in three sentences?
A plain summary is harder to hide behind than a long one.
Which part of your life is working well at the moment?
Start from what is solid.
Which part of your life have you been neglecting?
You usually already know.
What is missing from your life right now?
This is the question most people skip. Be specific.
What are you putting up with?
Small things you tolerate add up to a mood.
What does an ordinary good day look like for you?
Good years are built out of ordinary days.
What do you do every week that you would like to stop?
Stopping one thing frees more time than any new habit.
What do you wish you had more time for?
Write it down so you can see whether next year makes room for it.
Who do you want to be closer to?
A name is more useful here than a category.
How is your health, honestly?
Think about your body, your sleep and your mood.
How do you feel about your work when you wake up on a Monday?
The feeling tells you more than the job title.
What are you avoiding thinking about?
Naming it is half the work.
What would you try next year if you knew nobody would judge you?
It separates what you want from what looks sensible.
If the next twelve months went well, what would be different by this time next year?
This is the bridge from looking back to making a plan.
What is the one change that would improve most of the rest?
Your answer is a good candidate for next year's single focus.
